citation: Terry, Krista P., & Peter E. Doolittle. (2019). Re-examining Social Presence: Implications for Digital Pedagogies. Technology, Instruction, Cognition and Learning, 11, 121–139.
discipline: education / educational technology (social presence theory; digital pedagogies)
thesis: Social presence theory, despite three generations of development since Short, Williams & Christie's (1976) medium-based definition, still lacks a stable, widely accepted definition; tracing that evolution and synthesizing the models/measures literature, the paper argues social presence should instead be identified and tested as a non-mediated psychological construct — built from five factors (group cohesion, co-presence/salience of others, affective association, immediacy, intimacy) — so that a stable definition can, in turn, support more accurate measurement of social presence's impact on learning across both mediated and non-mediated instructional environments.

sections.title: Introduction: mediated vs. non-mediated presence
sections.summary: Defines social presence after Short, Williams & Christie (1976) as a sense of being with others in a technologically-mediated environment, then follows Lee (2004) in distinguishing mediated presence (perceptions transported by technology) from non-mediated presence (a purely psychological state, regardless of setting). Illustrates the unresolved-mechanism problem via Weidlich & Bastiaens's (2017) SIPS model. States the paper's goal: trace the concept's history and synthesize the literature toward a more stable, cross-environment definition.

sections.title: Digital pedagogy and social presence
sections.summary: Situates social presence within the broader push (Morris 2013; Wadmany & Kliachko 2014) for digital pedagogues to move beyond LMS-bound instruction. Uses Bronack et al.'s (2008) 3D virtual-campus project — which coined 'Presence Pedagogy' after students reported feeling co-present with peers — as an exemplar. Cites Richardson, Maeda, Lv & Caskurlu's (2017) meta-analysis finding positive but highly variable correlations between social presence and course satisfaction/perceived learning.

sections.title: History of social presence: three phases
sections.summary: Following Cui et al. (2013) and Lowenthal (2010), divides the field into three generational phases: Phase 1 (1970s-80s, Short, Williams & Christie's medium-based definition), Phase 2 (1990-1999, media-appropriateness critiques: Rutter's Cuelessness Theory, Daft & Lengel's Media Richness Theory, Walther's Social Information Processing Theory), Phase 3 (2000-present, the Community of Inquiry model and its later teaching/cognitive/learning-presence extensions).

sections.title: Definitions and measures: models overview
sections.summary: Reviews five foundational models: Gunawardena & Zittle's (1997) Social Presence Scale (14 bipolar items, grounded in intimacy/immediacy); Tu's (2002) Social Presence and Privacy Questionnaire and Tu & McIsaac's (2002) four relational dimensions; the Rourke/Garrison/Archer-derived Community of Inquiry model (social presence as projecting oneself as a 'real person'); Biocca, Harms & Burgoon's (2003) call for conceptual clarity; Sung & Mayer's (2012) Online Social Presence Questionnaire (five affective facets).

sections.title: Charting the course: five factors
sections.summary: Proposes testing social presence in a non-mediated setting via five factors distilled from the review: group cohesion, co-presence/salience of others, affective association, immediacy, and intimacy — framed as the psychological 'roots' of social presence, testable independent of any specific medium.

sections.title: Conclusion: implications of re-examining social presence
sections.summary: Endorses Kim et al.'s (2016) view that social presence occurs independent of any specific technology. Calls for measuring it across instructional environments, pedagogical approaches, student populations, academic domains, and cultural contexts. Raises an open question about whether social presence is independent of the Community of Inquiry's cognitive-teaching-social presence triad, and closes with a validity chain: valid measurement leads to accurately described impact, which leads to effective instructional interventions.

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: central construct; argued to be inconsistently measured because never isolated from the medium in which it is studied; decomposed into five sub-factors rather than treated as monolithic — this cluster's primary row-axis fill for this unit

constructs.label: group cohesion (sub-factor)
constructs.treatment: team/community capacity to work together toward shared tasks/goals; drawn from Garrison/Anderson/Archer (1999) and Rovai (2002) community definitions, and Whiteside's (2015) social-presence model elements (resource sharing, cohesive whole, approachability)

constructs.label: co-presence / salience of others (sub-factor)
constructs.treatment: a clear sense of who else is present, regardless of setting; drawn from Biocca/Harms/Burgoon and de Greef & IJsselsteijn's (2000) 'sense of being together'; Kreijns et al.'s (2010) immediate/delayed communication-episode distinction

constructs.label: affective association (sub-factor)
constructs.treatment: warmth/safety enabling free interaction; rooted in Short et al.'s (1976) bipolar semantic-differential scales; Whiteside's (2015) affective-association expansion of the Rourke/Garrison/Archer coding scale

constructs.label: immediacy (sub-factor)
constructs.treatment: verbal/nonverbal closeness behaviors reducing psychological/physical distance (Mehrabian 1971); Gunawardena & Zittle's (1997) teacher-immediacy behaviors; Garrison (2011) on risk-reduction and critical discourse

constructs.label: intimacy (sub-factor)
constructs.treatment: personalization and communication equilibrium; rooted in Argyle & Dean's (1965) eye-contact studies; Lombard & Ditton's (1997) expanded list of intimacy behaviors

constructs.label: community of inquiry (THEORY-MODEL, related but distinct)
constructs.treatment: reviewed as one of five foundational models; its 'real people' definition of social presence used as a touchstone, but its entanglement of social/cognitive/teaching/learning presence judged in the authors' own voice to have 'broadened and arguably convoluted' the field's definitional clarity — the article's most direct engagement with ped-sec-26

constructs.label: interactivity
constructs.treatment: distinguished from, not folded into, social presence: citing Picciano (2002), users may be highly interactive without feeling 'present,' even though many studies treat the two as near-synonyms

conditionsNote: Empty by design. This is a historical/theoretical literature review tracing definitions and measures of social presence across three generational phases; it reports no original sample, N, instrument validation, or statistical findings of its own — all empirical results cited (Weidlich & Bastiaens's SIPS finding, Richardson et al.'s meta-analytic correlations, Gunawardena & Zittle's and Sung & Mayer's factor-analytic results) are reported secondhand as background evidence. The paper's central conceptual move — arguing social presence should be measured in a non-mediated setting — is a proposal about the construct's psychological locus, not a tested media condition: no IVR/desktop-3D/2D contrast, home-vs-classroom comparison, or conventional-instruction control arm appears. Strand F is not required to populate the media-condition axis per plan scope, and nothing in this source genuinely fits any of the eight canonical column labels.

readings.claim: Despite multiple generations of theoretical development since Short, Williams & Christie's (1976) definition, social presence still lacks a stable, widely accepted definition.

Recasting social presence as a non-mediated psychological construct rather than a mediated/technological attribute shifts research attention from media affordances toward instructional and individual differences in generating and benefiting from social presence.

Weidlich & Bastiaens's (2017) SIPS-model finding — a sociable learning environment fosters social interaction, leading to social presence and a sound social space, in turn explaining learning-experience quality — begs unanswered questions about the instructional and individual-difference mechanisms linking social interaction, social presence, and learning.

Richardson, Maeda, Lv & Caskurlu's (2017) meta-analysis found positive but highly variable correlations between social presence and course satisfaction/perceived learning across discipline, course length, and audience, motivating the need for a more stable definition.

Social presence theory divides into three generational phases: a medium-based Phase 1 (1970s-80s), a media-appropriateness-critique Phase 2 (1990-1999), and a Community-of-Inquiry-situated online-learning Phase 3 (2000-present).

The Community of Inquiry model's entanglement of social presence with cognitive presence, teaching presence, and (later) learning presence broadened and, in the authors' own assessment, arguably convoluted the construct's definition.
Interactivity and social presence are not synonymous constructs, even though many studies continue to treat them as such; users can be highly interactive without feeling 'present.'

Five factors — group cohesion, co-presence/salience of others, affective association, immediacy, and intimacy — are the most critical contributors to learning environments high in social presence, derived from a literature review responding to Biocca et al.'s (2003) call to address unmediated as well as mediated interaction.

Once social presence is validly measured as a non-mediated psychological construct, its impact on variables of interest can be accurately described; once accurately described, effective instructional interventions can be created.

Whether social presence is independent of the Community of Inquiry's cognitive-teaching-social presence triad — and, if so, whether cognitive and teaching presence are independent of one another — is left as an open, unresolved question.

concepts.definition: Lee's (2004) distinction between perceptions transported/facilitated by technology (mediated) and perceptions that are direct, natural, and purely psychological regardless of setting (non-mediated); the article's central reframing device.

A sense of being with others in a virtual or technologically-mediated environment (after Short, Williams & Christie, 1976), traced through three generational redefinitions to the present psychological-construct proposal.
Gunawardena & Zittle's (1997) 14 bipolar-scale instrument grounded in intimacy (Argyle & Dean, 1965) and immediacy (Wiener & Mehrabian, 1968).
Tu's (2002) instrument isolating social context, online communication, interactivity, system privacy, and feeling of privacy as factors related to social presence.
Sung & Mayer's (2012) instrument isolating five affective facets: social respect, social sharing, open mind, social identity, and intimacy.
Terry & Doolittle's own proposed decomposition — group cohesion, co-presence/salience of others, affective association, immediacy, intimacy — framed as testable independent of medium.
Term coined by Bronack et al. (2008) to describe students' felt co-presence with peers in a 3D virtual-campus graduate program, cited as an exemplar of technology-enabled social presence.
Weidlich & Bastiaens's (2017) model relating sociability, social interaction, social presence, and social space.

tensions.axis: presence as technology-determined (medium properties) vs. presence as psychologically/individually determined (non-mediated construct)
tensions.note: The article's central argument and its most direct landing on the cluster's debate axis 3: explicitly sides with the psychological-construct pole while acknowledging the entangled middle ground occupied by the Community of Inquiry model.

tensions.axis: mediated-only measurement is sufficient vs. non-mediated baseline measurement is necessary
tensions.note: Lee (2004) and Biocca et al. (2001) are reported as arguing non-mediated measurement is unnecessary (too broad in scope, or self-evident); Terry & Doolittle explicitly contend it is imperative as a first step toward a stable, generalizable definition.

tensions.axis: social presence as independent of vs. entangled with cognitive/teaching presence (the Community of Inquiry triad)
tensions.note: Raised as an explicit open question in the conclusion and left unresolved by the article itself.

bridgeNote: The paper's co-presence/salience-of-others factor (a clear sense of who else is present, feeling 'together' regardless of setting) plausibly instantiates in the VLE's own survey/exemplar data. Per the VLE-proximity-voice correction on file, the VLE implements spatial-proximity voice co-watching with mandatory group assignment, which bears directly on vle-01's F7 finding (APP/VID presence-indicator gap, optative 'seemed isolating' language) and on vle-03's exemplar quotes about presence, carry-over, and social co-watching experience. The article's own theoretical move — locating social presence in a non-mediated psychological state rather than a technology byproduct — offers Part III a resource for interpreting the VLE's APP/VID presence gap without attributing it to the video medium's technological 'leanness' alone. The five-factor decomposition (group cohesion, co-presence, affective association, immediacy, intimacy) also offers a finer-grained vocabulary than a monolithic 'social presence' survey item would allow, useful if Part III's discussion wants to distinguish which of the five roots the VLE's design most directly cultivates (all P/anticipatory-application).
hubNote: Strand F's densest citation hub after ped-sec-26: directly engages Short/Williams/Christie, Gunawardena & Zittle, Tu & McIsaac, Biocca/Harms/Burgoon, Sung & Mayer, Garrison/Anderson/Archer (ped-sec-26), Richardson et al., and this cluster's Lombard & Ditton (ped-sec-01) and Witmer & Singer (ped-sec-02). Its engagement with ped-sec-26 is the article's most substantive single interlocutor relationship: it uses the CoI model's 'real people' definition as a touchstone while explicitly criticizing the model's entanglement of social/cognitive/teaching presence as having 'broadened and arguably convoluted' the field — both extending and contesting ped-sec-26's framework rather than simply endorsing it.
